extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry, drama, and playwriting (esp. classical/tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plots, characters, diction, song, spectacle) based on Aristotle's Poetics; aimed at building effective tragic plots and their constituent parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core defining criterion: tragedy imitates action (not men per se), aims to arouse pity and fear and to effect catharsis. All other features of a tragedy serve this end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity/Limit of Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun; whereas the Epic action has no limits of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic action should be roughly circumscribed in time to preserve unity and plausibility; epic may ignore such limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality — namely, Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These six elements are the basic evaluative dimensions; two (Song, Diction) constitute the medium of imitation, one the manner, and three the objects of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the imitation of the action:—by plot is meant the arrangement of the incidents; it is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the most important element; a well-constructed plot (arrangement of incidents) is more decisive than excellence in diction or character for producing tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as a Whole: beginning, middle, end
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end: a beginning does not itself follow anything by causal necessity, an end follows something but has nothing following it, a middle follows and is followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must conform to these causal principles; it must neither begin nor end at haphazard. Structure must respect causal necessity or rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Magnitude and Order
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful object (including a plot) must be of a certain magnitude and so arranged; there must be a length which can be embraced by memory and which admits a change from bad fortune to good, or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots too short (confused in an instant) or too vast (cannot be grasped at once). Magnitude contributes to beauty when the whole remains perspicuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in the imitation of one action which is a whole, structured such that if any one part is displaced the whole is disturbed; unity does not mean including all incidents of a hero's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse unity of action with narrating an entire life; select and shape incidents so they form one organic action with necessary/probable connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality and Probability (poetry vs history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry represents what may happen (possible according to law of probability or necessity) and thus expresses the universal; history relates what has happened (the particular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots should be driven by probability/necessity (cause-effect) rather than mere chronological narration of events; the poet's aim is the universal truth embodied in plausible actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Episodic Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'epeisodic' plot is one in which episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such plots are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: composing as a sequence of show-pieces or disconnected incidents (often to please players) undermines unity and tragic effect; maintain natural continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple when change of fortune occurs without Reversal (peripeteia) and without Recognition (anagnorisis); Complex when the change is accompanied by Reversal or Recognition or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that derive reversal/recognition from the internal structure of the plot are generally superior; decide whether to aim for simple continuity or complex causal surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of the Situation is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to the rule of probability or necessity (example: messenger intended to cheer Oedipus reveals his identity and causes opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal to produce striking emotional shift; it must arise naturally from the plot's causal structure, not by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; the best recognition coincides with a Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition ideally arises from the plot's internal logic and, when paired with reversal, produces the strongest pity/fear (e.g., Oedipus). Can be of persons or of facts/objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action (e.g., death on stage, bodily agony, wounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such scenes function as a distinct part of plot impact; use them when integral to the action's consequences and emotional effect, not merely for shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character's role and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents; character reveals moral purpose and is secondary to plot—actions, not character alone, make persons happy or the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must have consistent qualities revealed by choices; speeches that do not manifest choice/avoidance are not expressive of character. Character supports and arises from action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances—where something is proved or a general maxim enunciated; in oratory it corresponds to the function of rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought appears where arguments, proofs, or maxims are expressed; it should serve the action and reveal reasoning relevant to situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose. 'Language embellished' means language into which rhythm, harmony, and song enter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction comprises word choice and metrical/ornamental features; parts of the play may be rendered through verse alone or with song. Good diction should serve clarity and the imitation of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as Embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song holds the chief place among the embellishments; it is a term whose sense everyone understands and contributes to tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song is part of the medium of imitation and can be used to heighten emotional effect; integrate song where it naturally fits the parts of the play (choric/actor songs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle as a Less Artistic Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacular equipment and stage-effects are part of Tragedy and have emotional attraction, but of all the parts it is the least artistic and least connected with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can augment feeling but relies more on stagecraft than on poetic skill; do not substitute spectacle for properly constructed plot, character, and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Parts (Prologue, Episode, Exode, Parode, Stasimon, Commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue (before the Parode), Episode (between complete choric songs), Exode (final part with no choric song after it); Choric parts include Parode (first utterance), Stasimon (choric ode without specific meters), and Commos (chorus+actors lament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal divisions define where narrative, dialogue, and choric lyric should occur; use them to organize the unfolding of plot, song, and spectacle coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as Maker of Plots (Role of the Poet)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet or 'maker' should be the maker of plots rather than of verses; since he imitates actions, he is a poet when events (even historical) conform to probability/possibility and are shaped into universal patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot construction and causal shaping of events over purely rhetorical or verbal display; the poet's primary skill is in composing plausible, unified actions.
